claims.text: Controlled doping of an oxide support modulates charge transfer at the metal-support interface.
A change in support-induced charge transfer shifts the d-band center of the supported transition-metal nanoparticles.
Shifting the metal d-band center tunes the adsorption energies of key reaction intermediates.
Optimization of intermediate adsorption energies can enhance catalytic performance.
PtPdCoCuNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can be uniformly dispersed on an undoped oxide support.
The nanoparticle size, composition, and dispersion can be held constant while the oxide support is doped.
Nb or Ti doping modifies the electronic properties of the oxide support.
Charge transfer within PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles can modulate the electronic structure of Pt and Pd active sites.
Electronic-structure modulation can promote reactant adsorption and enhance catalytic activity.
Optimal adsorption energies can facilitate key reaction steps or prevent catalyst deactivation.
Relative to an undoped support, a doped support will produce both a shifted nanoparticle d-band center and enhanced catalytic performance.
The proposed causal relationship applies when nanoparticle size, dispersion, and composition remain constant under typical transition-metal catalytic conditions.
Extreme pH or very high temperature can induce additional catalyst restructuring.
The magnitude and performance effect of the d-band-center shift may depend on dopant identity, dopant concentration, and reaction conditions.
XPS or DRIFTS can quantify the proposed shift in the nanoparticle d-band center.
The controlled comparison consists of otherwise identical nanoparticles on undoped and doped oxide supports tested under identical reaction conditions.
